summary:
Ghosts of the Solar System is an interactive, story-driven web experience that introduces school-age and casual space enthusiasts to the hardware NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. Users choose a world, tap a glowing marker, and hear each machine tell its own story in the first person, from the Apollo 15 rover parked with its camera aimed at the sky to Insight listening to Mars’s heartbeat until its power faded. Each story pairs the engineering of the machine with the scientific discoveries it made possible, such as Opportunity’s evidence of ancient water or Pioneer 10’s first close-up views of Jupiter.

It addresses the challenge by turning dense mission histories into short, personal narratives rather than lists of facts. Most people hear only about active missions, so these stories show that silent explorers helped pave the way for today’s achievements. The page is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, works on phones and desktops, supports keyboard navigation, and respects light, dark, and reduced-motion settings.

It matters because stories make science memorable, and curiosity about past missions can inspire the next generation of explorers.
details:
An interactive web page where NASA’s retired machines tell their own stories. Pick the Moon, Mars, or Deep Space, tap a marker, and read a first-person story with what the machine discovered and a fun fact. It covers 8 machines.
It turns complex mission history into short, memorable stories for students and casual space fans. It works in any browser, on phones and computers, with no download needed, and it supports keyboard use and light and dark mode
To show young people that missions don’t end when the signal stops, and to inspire curiosity about past and future space exploration.
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a single file, a code editor and browser, Netlify or GitHub Pages for hosting, Google Slides or PowerPoint for the demo, and public NASA mission information. We also used an AI assistant (Claude) for drafting, and our team reviewed the results. Check this against the Space Apps rules on AI use.
Each machine speaks in its own voice, so facts become characters and stories. Pulsing markers act like waiting signals, and Voyager 1 appears as a “still talking” contrast to the silent ghosts. Audience age (8–14), accuracy against NASA records, accessibility, a lightweight format that works anywhere, and a data structure that makes adding new stories easy.
